title: Conditionals
summary: A conditional lets a program choose what to do based on a value.

subtopics.title: if
subtopics.explanation: An `if` block runs when its condition is truthy. For example, check whether a required field is present before sending a form. Use braces so the controlled statements are easy to see. If the condition combines several ideas, give each one a clear name or split the decision into smaller checks. Conditions can test comparisons, booleans, or truthy values. For fields and numeric boundaries, explicit comparisons often make the rule clearer to someone new to the code. An if statement is like taking a path only when a sign says it is open.

subtopics.title: else
subtopics.explanation: An `else` block handles the path when the preceding condition is false. It can show a validation message or choose a safe fallback. For example, an empty password field can produce a message that explains what the person should enter. Avoid duplicating large blocks; move shared behavior into a function. Keep the alternate path useful: explain what is missing and how to proceed. Avoid an empty else that hides a state the product should handle. An else branch is like the other route when the first path is closed.

subtopics.title: else if
subtopics.explanation: `else if` checks another condition after earlier conditions are false. Checks run in order, so put specific cases before broad cases. For example, check an administrator role before a general signed-in state. Otherwise, the broad branch may capture the value and make the specific branch unreachable. When cases overlap, order them from specific to general. Test a value that matches the boundary between branches, not only a typical value. An else-if chain is like checking several doors in order until one fits.

subtopics.title: Conditions
subtopics.explanation: A comparison such as `score >= passingScore` creates a true-or-false result. Conditions should explain the decision in terms a teammate can understand. If the same test appears several times, name it—for example, `canSubmit`—then use that name consistently instead of repeating a long expression. Named booleans make complex policy easier to review, especially when permissions or validation combine multiple requirements. A comparison is like asking whether a measurement meets a marked threshold.

subtopics.title: switch
subtopics.explanation: `switch` selects among cases for one value, such as a request status. Each case needs a clear exit or deliberate fall-through. Include a safe default when unexpected values are possible. A TypeScript exhaustive check can also reveal when a new state has no handling. Use a default branch to handle unexpected values safely. In TypeScript, an exhaustive check can make new cases visible during development. A switch is like matching one label to a route on a directory.

foundations.overview: Conditionals let JavaScript choose which code to run based on a true-or-false test. They help a program respond to values, such as showing a message when a form is incomplete. Think of them like signposts at a fork in a path. Keep conditions clear, order related cases carefully, and handle the path when no condition matches.
foundations.whyItMatters: Conditionals express product rules in code. Clear ordering and meaningful branches help prevent permissions, validation, or loading logic from choosing the wrong path.
foundations.browserPerspective: The engine coerces each condition to a boolean (ToBoolean) and jumps to the matching branch, skipping the others. switch compares with strict equality and, without break, simply continues into subsequent cases because there's no implicit boundary between them.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Form validation, feature flags, routing, loading/empty/error UI states, permission checks, and React conditional rendering all run on conditionals — often a mix of if guards, ternaries in JSX, and && short-circuits.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct branching is the difference between a feature that handles every state gracefully and one that crashes or shows the wrong screen; conditional bugs directly produce visible product defects.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Guard clauses and well-structured conditionals keep functions readable and reviewable, while missing break statements and deep nesting create fragile code that's hard to change safely.
foundations.performanceImpact: Branching itself is fast; the practical performance lever is ordering conditions so the cheapest or most common case is checked first, and using switch (or lookup objects) instead of long if/else chains for many discrete values.
commonUseCases: Validating input and handling edge cases with guard clauses
Choosing UI states (loading, empty, error, success)
Mapping a single value to many outcomes with switch
Conditional rendering with && and ternaries in JSX

commonMisconceptions.myth: if conditions must be true/false booleans.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Any value works because JavaScript coerces it via truthy/falsy rules, so if (str) or if (arr.length) are valid and common.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Each switch case automatically stops at the next case.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Without break (or return), execution falls through into the following cases, which is a frequent bug.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A condition must always be written as a comparison.
commonMisconceptions.reality: JavaScript also tests truthy and falsy values, but explicit checks can be clearer for beginners.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The first matching branch should always be the broadest one.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Earlier broad checks can make later specific branches unreachable.

visualExplorer.title: How an if / else if / else chain is evaluated
visualExplorer.caption: Step through how JavaScript checks conditions in order and runs only the first matching branch.

config.intro: Follow a grading function as it decides which branch to run for a score of 85.

steps.name: Evaluate the first condition
steps.detail: The engine coerces `score >= 90` to a boolean. For 85 this is false, so the first block is skipped.

steps.name: Evaluate the else if
steps.detail: It moves to the next condition `score >= 80`, which is true for 85.

steps.name: Run the matching block
steps.detail: Because this branch matched, its block runs (logs 'B'), and all remaining branches are skipped.

steps.name: Skip the else
steps.detail: Once a branch has matched, the final else is never reached — only one branch ever executes.

steps.name: Continue after the chain
steps.detail: Execution resumes on the line after the whole if/else if/else, having taken exactly one path.

codeLab.title: Refactor nested ifs into guard clauses
codeLab.instructions: Rewrite getDiscount(user) using guard clauses so the happy path isn't deeply nested. Return 0 for a missing user or a missing membership, and return the member discount otherwise. Avoid an else after a return.
hints: Handle the invalid cases first and return early so the rest of the function isn't nested.
After an early return you don't need an else — the happy path can sit un-indented at the end.

keyTakeaways: An `if` block runs when its condition is truthy.
An `else` block handles the path when the preceding condition is false.
`else if` checks another condition after earlier conditions are false.
A comparison such as `score >= passingScore` creates a true-or-false result.
`switch` selects among cases for one value, such as a request status.
